summary:
Queensland is a state of Australia and stands under the national framework; the national record carries the federal law, and this record covers the state layer.

Gender identity has been a protected attribute under Queensland's Anti-Discrimination Act since 2002. Amendments that commenced on 29 April 2024 moved serious vilification out of that Act and into the Criminal Code, with a maximum penalty of three years' imprisonment, raised from six months. The same amendments explicitly extend protection to non-binary and gender-diverse people and broaden the definition of gender identity. The Queensland Human Rights Commission described the Anti-Discrimination Bill 2024 as a rewrite that modernised the gender identity attribute and revised the vilification provisions.

Queensland was the first Australian state to criminalise conversion practices. The Health Legislation Amendment Bill 2019 passed the parliament on 13 August 2020, making practices including electro-shock, drug and hypnotherapy aimed at changing a person's sexuality or gender identity offences carrying fines and imprisonment for practitioners, with a maximum of 18 months. Survivors report that the ban does not reach conversion practices in informal, non-healthcare settings.

Access to gender-affirming care for minors has been restricted since January 2025. The health minister, Tim Nicholls, halted puberty blockers and hormone therapy for new public-system patients under 18 with gender dysphoria, formalised by a Queensland Health directive of 28 January 2025. The restriction remains in force and is legally contested. Patients already enrolled with the Queensland Children's Gender Service are exempt, so the practical effect falls on new patients and their families.

Queensland documents have carried an X non-binary option alongside male and female since 1 September 2021, including marriage certificates and official forms. Transgender and intersex residents can update government records and their birth certificate; the requirement to divorce before changing a record was repealed in 2018 and the surgery requirement was repealed in 2024.

State law recognises relationships through civil partnership registration or an unregistered de facto relationship, recognised since 2002. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under birth-sex status can register a civil partnership or rely on de facto recognition in the same way as any other couple.

The state's criminal-law regime has been progressively liberalised. Private consensual sex between men has been legal since 1991, and lesbian sexual acts were never criminalised. The age of consent was equalised at 16 for all sexual acts in 2016, Queensland being the last Australian jurisdiction to do so; the former section 208 carried up to 14 years' imprisonment for anal sex involving a person under 18. The gay panic defence was abolished from the criminal law in 2017.
tangentialFactors:
The conversion-practices offence is confined to health-care settings as described in the reporting. Survivors say informal and non-healthcare practices fall outside it, so the protection is narrower than the ban's scope suggests.

Equality Australia described Queensland as an outlier among Australian states for the under-18 care restriction, a characterisation that places the measure against the direction of policy elsewhere in the country.
localsOnly:
Residents who change their recorded gender can obtain a new birth certificate and updated government records; the surgery requirement was repealed in 2024 and the divorce requirement in 2018.

Same-sex couples may become parents through adoption, foster care and altruistic surrogacy, and lesbian couples through IVF; eligibility to adopt dates from 11 November 2016.

Convictions for consensual homosexual acts can be expunged under a law passed in 2017 and in effect from 30 June 2018.

Serious vilification sits in the Criminal Code rather than the Anti-Discrimination Act following the 2024 amendments, so complaints of that kind go through the criminal process.

Under the January 2025 directive, patients already enrolled with the Queensland Children's Gender Service keep access to puberty blockers and hormone therapy; new patients under 18 must obtain treatment privately, at costs families report as hundreds of dollars per injection and nearly $2,000 in one case.
outOfScopeNotes:
The Queensland Human Rights Commission's own announcement of the April 2024 changes is no longer reachable, so the account of that rewrite rests on secondary reporting and the record held here.

No enforcement data for the serious vilification offence, whether prosecutions, convictions or sentences, appears in the sources consulted.

The sources do not state whether the under-18 restriction on public-system care affects adult patients, or how it applies to young people visiting Queensland from elsewhere.

Several details of the state's legal history rest on a tertiary encyclopaedic source rather than on the instruments themselves.

The scope of the conversion-practices ban outside health-care settings is reported through survivors' accounts and is not resolved by the sources consulted.
